items.title: Equal temperament's compromise
items.claim: 12-tone equal temperament (12-TET) makes all keys playable. What does it sacrifice compared to just intonation?

options.text: All intervals except the octave are slightly out of tune relative to pure ratios
It only works for one key

items.reveal_title: Every interval except the octave is mistuned
items.reveal:
12-TET divides the octave into 12 equal semitones of 100 cents each. The perfect fifth is about 2 cents flat from the pure 3:2 ratio; the major third is around 14 cents sharp from 5:4.

Most Western fixed-pitch instruments since the 19th century use it.
items.why: A practical standard often involves giving up purity for portability across keys.

items.title: When Schoenberg formalised twelve-tone technique
items.claim: Arnold Schoenberg's 'method of composing with twelve tones related only to one another' was first described publicly in approximately which year?
items.reveal_title: The technique was described in the early 1920s
items.reveal:
Schoenberg discussed the technique with students around 1921-1923; his Suite for Piano Op. 25 (1923) is one of the first fully serial works.

Webern, Berg and later Boulez and Stockhausen extended the method.
items.why: Major shifts in musical language can be tracked to specific compositional methods.

items.title: The first jazz recording
items.claim: The Original Dixieland Jass Band made what is widely cited as the first commercially released jazz record in February 1917. What is notable about the band's identity?

options.text: It consisted of New Orleans-based white musicians, recording before any African American jazz band
It was the original Louis Armstrong Hot Five

items.reveal_title: An all-white band recorded jazz before the Black originators
items.reveal:
Recording technology and the racially segregated music industry meant the Original Dixieland Jass Band reached commercial release first.

Joe 'King' Oliver, Kid Ory and others were performing earlier; many of their performances were never recorded.
items.why: The historical record of an art form can systematically misrepresent who created it.

items.title: When A=440 became standard
items.claim: A=440 Hz is the modern reference tuning. When was it widely standardised internationally?
items.reveal_title: Standard pitch was agreed only in the 20th century
items.reveal:
An international conference in London in May 1939 recommended A=440 Hz; ISO 16:1955 confirmed it.

Historical performance practice often uses A=415 Hz (Baroque) or other regional standards.
items.why: Absolute pitch references are conventions that have shifted across centuries.

items.title: How tape changed composition
items.claim: Magnetic tape recording became widely available in the late 1940s. Which composer used it to develop musique concrete in 1948?
items.reveal_title: Schaeffer's Etude aux chemins de fer, 1948
items.reveal:
Schaeffer used recorded train sounds to compose at RTF, Paris. The studio later became GRM (Groupe de Recherches Musicales).

The method established sound itself, separated from its source, as compositional material.
items.why: Recording media are not just preservation tools; they create new compositional possibilities.

items.title: What 'Well-Tempered' meant
items.claim: J.S. Bach's The Well-Tempered Clavier (1722, 1742) covers all 24 major and minor keys. Was Bach writing for equal temperament?

options.text: Probably a well temperament (such as Werckmeister or Kirnberger) where all keys were usable but each had different colour

items.reveal:
Scholarship suggests Bach used a well temperament such as those proposed by Werckmeister, where each key sounded subtly distinct.

Lehman's 2005 proposal even reads the cover ornament as encoding a specific tuning.
items.why: Historical performance research recovers sounds standard recordings obscure.

items.title: Streaming payouts per stream
items.claim: Reported per-stream payouts from Spotify to rights holders in the early 2020s are roughly which range?
items.reveal_title: Fractions of a cent per stream
items.reveal:
Industry reports and Spotify's Loud and Clear site indicate average per-stream rates of about $0.003 to $0.005, with substantial variation between rights holders and territories.

From 2024 Spotify required tracks to reach 1,000 streams in 12 months before generating royalties at all.
items.why: The economics of recorded music differ fundamentally between physical and streaming eras.

items.title: Cage's 4'33 in 1952
items.claim: John Cage's 4'33 was first performed at Woodstock, NY in 1952. What is true of the score?

options.text: It instructs the performer to make no intentional sound for three movements totalling 4 minutes 33 seconds
It is a recording of silence

items.reveal:
David Tudor premiered the piece on 29 August 1952 at the Maverick Concert Hall.

Cage said his point was that no environment is ever silent; the audience's coughs, the rustle of trees and the room itself become the work.
items.why: Defining what counts as music expands the analytical toolkit for understanding sound.

items.title: The Mozart effect
items.claim: The 'Mozart effect' became famous after a 1993 Nature paper. What did the original study actually report?

options.text: Listening to Mozart permanently raised children's IQ
A short, narrow improvement on a spatial reasoning task in adults, lasting about 10-15 minutes

items.reveal_title: A short-lived effect on one specific task in adults
items.reveal:
Rauscher, Shaw and Ky (1993) reported a brief improvement on the Stanford-Binet paper-folding task in adult students.

The finding became 'classical music makes babies smarter' in popular media; later meta-analyses (Pietschnig et al., 2010) found little support for that broader claim.
items.why: Translating a careful experimental finding into public policy often loses its caveats.

items.title: When Vivaldi was rediscovered
items.claim: After Vivaldi's death in 1741 his music largely disappeared from concert programmes. When did serious revival begin?

options.text: Within ten years of his death
The 1920s-1950s, after manuscript discoveries in Turin

items.reveal:
Manuscripts found in monastic libraries reached the Biblioteca Nazionale di Torino in the 1920s-1930s. Recording, especially after 1950, restored Vivaldi to the canon.

The Four Seasons (1725) is now among the most recorded works in classical music.
items.why: Canonical status is reconstructed, not fixed; archival luck matters.

items.title: How long the Beatles recorded
items.claim: From the first EMI recording session to the band's official break-up, roughly how long did the Beatles record together?
items.reveal_title: About 8 years from first session to break-up
items.reveal:
First EMI session: 6 June 1962. Paul McCartney's public departure announcement: 10 April 1970. Twelve UK studio albums in that period.

George Martin produced almost all of them at Abbey Road.
items.why: Cultural impact and recording duration are not the same thing.
